intro_text:
Coney Island Beach is a free public beach in southern Brooklyn. NYC Parks runs it from West 37th Street to Ocean Parkway and describes the beach as nearly three miles of sand. The city maintains 14 miles of beach in all. A 2.7-mile boardwalk runs behind the sand, a short walk from Stillwell Avenue, the last stop on the D, F, N and Q trains. Lifeguards are on duty from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. every day of the beach season. In 2026 the season ran from Saturday, May 23 to September 13, so swimming is closed now. The city says its beaches reopen Memorial Day weekend 2027. When the season is on, swim only in sections that are open, and only while lifeguards are on duty. Red flags and signs mark the closed sections.

You can still walk the sand and the boardwalk when swimming is closed. Walking, running and sitting on the beach are allowed during park hours. The boardwalk closes each night from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. In May 2026, Parks Commissioner Tricia Shimamura said Coney Island is the only city beach where Parks runs a 24-hour operation.

Coney Island is famous for what was built behind the sand. From about 1880 to World War II it was the largest amusement area in the United States, drawing several million visitors a year, according to Wikipedia's history of the neighborhood. Three big parks led the way: Steeplechase, opened in 1897; Luna Park, opened in 1903; and Dreamland. People came by train, and after 1920 by a five-cent subway ride. Fire destroyed Dreamland in 1911 and much of Luna Park in 1944. Steeplechase closed in 1964 and was bulldozed in 1966.

The beach went the other way. Private owners once fenced some stretches of it into the water. In 1912 only one street, West 23rd, gave the public a direct path from Surf Avenue to the sand. A 1913 court ruling said the beach belonged to the state. The city then built the boardwalk, added 1.7 million cubic yards of sand to widen the beach, and opened it on May 15, 1923. In the Great Depression, Wikipedia says, Luna Park could not compete with a beach “which charged no admission.” The parks are gone. The free beach is still here.

A few pieces of the old days still stand: the Wonder Wheel from 1920, the Cyclone roller coaster from 1927, and the steel tower of the Parachute Jump. Around them are Luna Park's newer rides, the New York Aquarium, a minor-league ballpark and Nathan's hot dog stand on its 1916 corner. Summer still brings the Mermaid Parade, which ends at the water to open the swimming season, and the Fourth of July hot dog eating contest. This page covers the beach day first, then the story of the parks, then the hard parts a visitor should know.
spike_explainer:
Coney Island had three big amusement parks: Steeplechase, Luna Park and Dreamland. All three are gone. Fire, money trouble and bulldozers took them between 1911 and 1966. The public beach in front of them is still free and still open. The Luna Park open today is a newer park that opened in 2010. This is how that happened.

**Before the big parks**

People came to this sand long before the big rides. A railroad first reached Coney Island in 1864. In the 1870s, 35 cents bought a train ride on the Culver line to Surf Avenue. Large hotels went up at the east end. President Ulysses S. Grant presided at the opening of the Manhattan Beach Hotel in July 1877. Its developer, Austin Corbin, barred Jewish guests. On July 21, 1879, he gave his anti-Jewish interview to the New York Daily Herald. A local history site says the press and Christian clergy almost all condemned him. In 2007 the city renamed Corbin Place for a different Corbin: Margaret Corbin, a Revolutionary War patriot.

The early amusements were small and loose. A hotel shaped like an elephant had telescopes in its eyes. A Brooklyn Public Library history says it was working as a brothel by 1890. It burned on September 27, 1896. Sea Lion Park opened in 1895. Wikipedia calls it Coney Island's first amusement area to charge an entry fee.

**Steeplechase Park, 1897 to 1964**

George Tilyou saw the big Ferris wheel at the 1893 Chicago fair on his honeymoon. He came home and built a half-size copy on Surf Avenue. In 1897 he opened Steeplechase Park. It was meant for families. Drinking, gambling and prostitution were banned. Later he added a gate and a 25-cent admission charge to keep out the rougher crowd.

Early on July 29, 1907, a fire started in a ride called the Cave of the Winds. About 35 acres of Coney Island burned. The next morning Tilyou put up a sign: “Admission to the burning ruins - ten cents.” He paid to rebuild by selling 100,000 shares. Anyone who bought a $5 stock certificate got a season pass. The city had passed a law limiting wooden buildings, so he rebuilt in steel and concrete. The centerpiece was the Pavilion of Fun, a steel-and-glass hall 450 by 280 feet.

Steeplechase outlived its rivals, but not without harm. In 1933, fifty-seven people were hurt when an overcrowded balcony collapsed. A fire in September 1939 injured 18 people and did $200,000 in damage. In 1941 the owners, Frank Tilyou and George Tilyou Jr., brought in the Parachute Jump from the 1939 World's Fair. They paid $150,000 for it. Riders were pulled up a 250-foot tower and dropped under a parachute. Up to half a million people rode it each season.

War and race shaped the park too. In 1945, with men away in the draft, only 70 people worked at Steeplechase. In a normal year it took 300. In 1946 the operators of its pool used a season-pass system that, in Wikipedia's words, “effectively locked out African Americans from using the pool.”

Steeplechase closed for the last time on September 20, 1964. Marie Tilyou, the main stockholder, sold the family's Coney Island land to developer Fred Trump over the objections of her brothers and sisters. The website 6sqft dates the sale to February 1965. Untapped New York says 1964. Untapped also reports that Trump bid through a stand-in named Jimmy Onorato, hoping a hidden buyer would get a better price.

Steeplechase did not open for the 1965 season. In 1966 (the date 6sqft gives), while people were working to make it a landmark, Trump held a demolition party. Guests were invited to throw bricks at the front of Steeplechase. Untapped says he hired models in revealing outfits to parade out front, and that guests smashed the Pavilion of Fun's stained glass. Then he bulldozed the building at night. Untapped says this limited any pending landmark case. That motive has never been proven.

The steel tower was spared. Trump wanted to sell the Parachute Jump for scrap. He did not think it was old enough to be a landmark. Sources still disagree on when it last carried riders. Coney Island historian Charles Denson says 1964 and calls 1968 a repeated error. NYC Parks and engineer Helen Harrison say 1968. The Brooklyn Paper says 1965. The city voted in 1968 to buy the Steeplechase site for $4 million. In 1971 Parks tried to auction off the tower and got no bids. Today it is all that is left of Steeplechase.

Trump never got the zoning change he needed to build housing on the land. He leased it to Norman Kaufman, who ran a small kiddie park there. The city, which bought the site from Trump in 1969, ended that lease in 1981. Denson wrote that when Steeplechase “failed to open for the 1965 season,” the news “created a worldwide impression that the whole of Coney Island had closed.” A minor-league ballpark opened on the old grounds in 2001.

**Luna Park, 1903 to 1944**

Thompson and Dundy built Luna Park. Before it opened, in January 1903, they killed an elephant named Topsy on the site, first with electricity and then with cyanide. Wikipedia says Edison's film company recorded it.

At 8 p.m. on May 16, 1903, the park's lights came on. Five minutes later the gates opened to 45,000 people. Admission was ten cents, and some rides cost up to 25 cents more. On the Fourth of July that year, 142,000 people came. The owners had spent $700,000 but advertised the cost as $1 million. In less than three months they earned back 90 percent of it. By the late 1900s Luna Park drew five million guests a year.

One of Luna's first attractions was an infant incubator exhibit. Martin Couney kept premature babies alive in incubators and charged the public 25 cents to look. He never charged the parents. Doctors did not accept incubators until the 1930s, so Couney ran his care as a show. The Coney Island History Project says his Luna exhibit ran from 1903 until 1943. Arizona State University's Embryo Project says from 1904. Historians now believe he was not a medical doctor. The usual count, which traces back to Couney's own claims, is more than 8,000 babies treated and over 6,500 who lived. Lucille Horn, one of his babies in 1920, said later: “I think it was definitely more of a freak show.”

In the Great Depression, Wikipedia says, Luna Park could not compete with Coney Island's beach, “which charged no admission.” Three creditors filed a bankruptcy petition against it in 1933. In World War II it had to keep its lights dim for security. On August 13, 1944, a fire destroyed much of the park and did $800,000 in damage. Sources differ on when Luna Park finally closed. 6sqft says 1946. It never reopened as a full park. 6sqft says the land was razed and rezoned for housing in 1950.

**Dreamland, to 1911**

Dreamland was the third big park. It was running by 1904, when Couney opened a second incubator exhibit there. A fire destroyed Dreamland in 1911. The Brooklyn Paper says it began when light bulbs popped over workers who were sealing a leak in the Hellgate water ride with tar. The Brooklyn Paper also says a burning lion ran down Surf Avenue and climbed the Ben-Hur ride. The day after the fire, manager Samuel Gumpertz pitched a tent on the still-smoking ground and opened a sideshow. 6sqft says Robert Moses later moved the New York Aquarium onto the old Dreamland site to keep another amusement park from opening.

**The beach that stayed**

For most of the park years, the sand was not open to everyone. By the middle of the 19th century, private owners had split up the waterfront and put up barriers. Some fences ran into the water. One 1904 estimate put the public beachfront at 1.4 square inches for each of the city's 3.7 million people. In 1912 only one street, West 23rd, gave the public a direct path from Surf Avenue to the beach.

That year New York State sued the amusement owners for taking the beach as private property. In 1913 a judge ruled that the beach belonged to the state, not to Tilyou and the other owners. An appeals court agreed in 1916, with an exception for part of Steeplechase. The city broke ground on a boardwalk on October 1, 1921, the day it took title to the land. The street work condemned 288 lots, including 175 houses and part of Steeplechase. NYC Parks says the beach project took 1.7 million cubic yards of sand and added 2.5 million square feet of beach. The first part of the boardwalk opened in October 1922, and the full length opened on May 15, 1923. Borough President Riegelmann, whose name it carries, said that “poor people will no longer have to stand with their faces pressed against wire fences looking at the ocean.”

The new beach could hold more than half a million people, and it needed to. Once the subway reached Coney Island in 1920, the trip from the city cost a nickel. By then up to a million people filled the island on the hottest days. The Parks Department took over the boardwalk in 1938. Parks Commissioner Robert Moses said the beaches “were never properly planned” and complained that the contractor had been allowed to dump brown sand. Between 1938 and 1941, Parks covered the beach with a 2-foot layer of fine white sand. Wikipedia says Moses described the beach as so crowded that bathers had less room than in a coffin. The V&A dates a Weegee beach photograph, “Coney Island,” to 1940.

**What came after**

After the war, the city moved toward housing. On April 2, 1953, the New York Times reported that Moses had proposed rezoning Coney Island for homes. Low-income housing projects went up starting in 1954. A smaller space-themed park, Astroland, opened in 1962. In 1975 its owners took over the Cyclone, a 1927 wooden coaster the city had planned to tear down. Astroland closed on September 7, 2008. A new Luna Park opened on its site on May 29, 2010. In 2025 a state advisory panel voted 4 to 2 against advancing a $3 billion casino development beside the boardwalk.

Walk the boardwalk today and you can still read the old map. The Parachute Jump marks the Steeplechase grounds, and the ballpark stands on them. 6sqft says the aquarium stands on the old Dreamland site. The Wonder Wheel and the Cyclone still run. And the sand that people once looked at through wire fences is open to anyone who gets off the train.
honest_reckoning_note:
People drown here, and in two recent cases reported by the press, it happened in water that was closed to swimmers. On July 5, 2024, two sisters, ages 17 and 18, went into the water amid rip-current warnings after lifeguards had gone off duty. Police said they disappeared from view shortly after 8 p.m., two hours after the 6 p.m. end of lifeguard hours. Divers recovered them. On July 27, 2023, lifeguards saw two brothers in trouble in a no-swimming area near West 22nd Street. Parks said that section was under a red flag. A 14-year-old was pulled out alive. His 15-year-old brother was lost, and his body was found by July 30. In the days after, families were still wading in past the red flags. “We're just putting our feet in, we're not going too far. It's hot,” one told CBS.

Staffing limits where you can swim. In July 2023 the city had only 800 lifeguards for eight beaches and 48 pools. Then-Commissioner Sue Donoghue said Coney Island had guards at six bays, and other areas were closed. In May 2026 Brownstoner reported that in recent years shortages had closed sections of beach temporarily, and sometimes for weeks at a time.

The water is not always clean. After a week of heavy rain in July 2026, a sample taken at Coney Island on July 6 measured 227 enterococci per 100 milliliters. The New York State limit for a single sample is 104. ABC7 reported that the city warned people to stay out of the water at a dozen beaches. ABC7 said the advisory covered wading too, yet it found no announcements on the beach and only one small sign on the boardwalk. Enterococci usually do not cause illness on their own. They are a warning sign of fecal pollution and more dangerous germs.

Flooding is a real risk behind the beach. Hurricane Sandy took 600,000 cubic yards of sand off the beach in 2012. A local activist says the worst flooding came from Coney Island Creek, not the ocean. The Army Corps says the surge also pushed sand and water over the boardwalk. In 2021 EPA inspectors found cyanide and the banned ant poison mirex in the creek, on top of earlier findings of PCBs, lead and benzene. As of November 2023 it was still not a federal Superfund site. Sea level around New York City has risen about a foot since 1900. The city's climate panel projects another one to two feet by the 2050s.
reckoning_pullquote: “We don't need more people knowing how to work a blackjack table, we need lifeguards, we need teachers,” a resident told a Community Board 13 casino hearing in January 2025.

margin_notes.text: New for 2026: Parks gave lifeguards small utility vehicles so they can drive themselves and their gear across the sand to an emergency. Lifeguard recruits rose 23 percent in 2025 after a new union contract.

At the 2026 opening, Council Member Kayla Santosuosso called Coney Island “the people's beach... on this side of town.” Further east, at the end of the peninsula, Manhattan Beach is small and family-focused, with picnic tables and grills.

Dutch maps labeled the sand spit Conyne Eylandt starting with the 1639 Manatus map. A 1654 deed records the Lenape name narriockh as meaning simply “the island.” No theory of where the name Coney comes from has strong evidence.

Before Nathan's there was Feltman's. 6sqft reports that Charles Feltman started in 1867 pushing a pie wagon through the dunes. By the 1920s his place sold 40,000 hot dogs a day at ten cents each. It lasted until 1954.

Coney Island was once an island, separated by Coney Island Creek. Landowners had filled part of the creek by 1924. Belt Parkway work in the 1930s filled more, and fill from the 1962 Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge left the creek an inlet. It is now a peninsula.

From the mid-1970s, Soviet immigrants, mostly Jews from Russia and Ukraine, settled in neighboring Brighton Beach, which earned the nickname Little Odessa. Since the early 2010s many Central Asian immigrants have settled there too.

day_in_time.dawn: The boardwalk reopens at 5 a.m. after its nightly closing. Parks staff work here around the clock; Commissioner Shimamura said in 2026 that at any hour “you will see parkies out doing the jobs that they need to do.” In May and June, horseshoe crabs come out of the Atlantic onto Coney Island Beach to breed. They favor night high tides near the full and new moon, Parks says it is fine to flip a stranded crab back over. Never pick it up by the tail. In winter, the Polar Bear Club has swum every Sunday, in every weather, from November to April, its president said in 2014.
day_in_time.midday: Lifeguards are in the chairs from 10 a.m. in season. Soon after, Parks updates its online beach map to show which sections are open that day, based on how many guards are working and on conditions. Free SPF 30 sunscreen is offered at all eight city beaches. Away from the water there are courts for beach volleyball, handball and basketball. A Coney Island resident told CBS in 2023 that many buildings nearby have no air conditioning, so people go to the water to cool off. Brooklyn Borough Parks Commissioner Marty Maher joked at the 2026 opening that the Atlantic is the “biggest air conditioner in the world.”
day_in_time.golden: In season, the lifeguards leave at 6 p.m. and the water is closed for the day. On the Wonder Wheel, one turn takes ten minutes, and each ride is two turns. Sixteen of its 24 cabins slide along curving tracks as the wheel turns. The other eight stay fixed to the rim, and each kind has its own line. The Wonder Wheel's busiest day on record was July 4, 1947, when it carried 14,506 riders.
day_in_time.night: After dark the Parachute Jump can light up. Its frame carries about 8,000 light fixtures used for night light shows. The lights went on in 2006 and were replaced in 2013. The boardwalk stays open until 1 a.m. Shimamura remembers a late weeknight when the beach was packed with people walking, playing, holding snakes and doing magic tricks. The water is closed all night. Swimming is not allowed when lifeguards are off duty.

food_drink.name: Nathan's Famous, the original stand (founded 1916)
food_drink.description: Nathan Handwerker opened a nickel hot dog stand here in 1916 and undercut his old employer, Feltman's, which charged ten cents. To reassure wary customers, he had men in surgeon's smocks eat at the stand. Nathan's coined the phrase “kosher style” because its all-beef hot dogs were not under rabbinic supervision. The clam bar dates to 1946. Fried frog legs, on the menu since the 1950s, are still sold at this original location.
food_drink.source: Wikipedia - Nathan's Famous; Nathan's franchise history

food_drink.name: Totonno's Pizzeria Napolitana (founded 1924)
food_drink.description: Totonno's says it has made pizza the same way in the same spot since 1924, and calls itself the “oldest, continually run, family-owned pizzeria in America.” It bakes in a coal-fired brick oven. New coal ovens fail current city environmental law, so the old one is allowed only while the business stays open. It won a James Beard America's Classics award in 2009. The owners said in May 2024 that they were looking for a buyer, and no sale is confirmed. Call before you go.

zones.name: West end: West 37th to West 29th Streets
zones.character: The west end of the Parks beach, which starts at West 37th Street. Past it is Sea Gate, a gated community of about 8,000 residents with private beaches. A stone groin at West 37th Street holds the sand; in 2016 the Army Corps built four more stone groins at Sea Gate and placed 75,000 cubic yards of sand around them.
zones.best_for: The west end of the Parks beach, with mats at three street ends
zones.notes: Wheelchair mats and beach wheelchair pickup points are at West 33rd, West 32nd and West 29th Streets. Which sections are open for swimming changes day to day with lifeguard staffing; check the Parks beach map, updated soon after 10 a.m.

zones.name: Steeplechase grounds: West 22nd Street to the Parachute Jump
zones.character: The old Steeplechase Park land. The Parachute Jump stands on the boardwalk between West 16th and West 19th Streets, in Steeplechase Plaza, and Maimonides Park sits on the old park grounds. In 1912, West 23rd was the only street with a direct public path from Surf Avenue to the beach. After the Mermaid Parade, 6sqft says, the king and queen lead a procession to the beach at 19th Street to open the swimming season.
zones.best_for: The Parachute Jump, Cyclones games, the end of the Mermaid Parade
zones.notes: On July 27, 2023, the water near West 22nd Street was a no-swimming area under a red flag; it is where a 15-year-old went missing in the water that day; he was found dead by July 30. A wheelchair mat and pickup point are at West 22nd Street.

zones.name: Amusement district: Stillwell Avenue to West 10th Street
zones.character: Nathan's original stand is at Surf and Stillwell. Deno's Wonder Wheel Amusement Park is on Denos Vourderis Place, formerly West 12th Street; from Stillwell Avenue, head toward the beach, climb to the boardwalk, turn left and walk one block. Luna Park fills 1000 Surf Avenue at West 10th Street. In 2010 Parks proposed keeping wood only on the four-block boardwalk stretch between West 15th and West 10th Streets.
zones.notes: A wheelchair mat and pickup point are at Stillwell Avenue.

zones.name: Aquarium: West 8th to West 5th Streets
zones.character: The New York Aquarium's Sharks building hangs over the boardwalk, wrapped in an 1,100-foot moving wall of more than 33,000 aluminum flaps made with artist Ned Kahn. Outside the aquarium is a 332-foot, ten-foot-tall cast-concrete sculpture wall by Toshio Sasaki. The F and Q stop at West 8th Street-NY Aquarium.
zones.notes: Beach wheelchairs are picked up at West 8th Street and the boardwalk, opposite the aquarium. Mats are at West 8th and West 5th Streets.

zones.name: Ocean Parkway to Brighton 15th Street
zones.character: The Parks beach listing for Coney Island ends at Ocean Parkway, and Brighton Beach continues east on the same sand. Brownstoner calls Brighton the quieter, less touristy beach. In 2012 the city approved replacing the wooden boardwalk between Coney Island Avenue and Brighton 15th Street with concrete and recycled plastic lumber.
zones.best_for: A calmer beach day, walks east along the boardwalk
zones.notes: Wheelchair mats are at Ocean Parkway, Brighton 2nd and 6th Streets, Coney Island Avenue and Brighton 15th Street.

landmarks.name: Riegelmann Boardwalk
landmarks.description: The 2.7-mile boardwalk is 80 feet wide for most of its length and sits 13 or 14 feet above sea level. Sources differ on its first planks: Wikipedia says Douglas fir from Washington State, NYC Parks says long leaf yellow pine. In 1924 the city approved five comfort stations and five beachfront pavilions after the Comptroller said it was not a real boardwalk without them. In 2012 a city design panel voted 6-0 to replace wood between Coney Island Avenue and Brighton 15th Street with concrete and recycled plastic. A Parks designer said, “we would greatly prefer to use wood.”
landmarks.source: Wikipedia - Riegelmann Boardwalk; NYC Parks historical sign; Brooklyn Paper, 2012

landmarks.name: Deno's Wonder Wheel
landmarks.description: Denos Vourderis bought the wheel on June 7, 1983, for $250,000. The only handover instructions were two words, “good luck,” written on a cigarette box. The wheel stopped on its own just once, in the July 13, 1977 blackout, when the owners cranked it by hand to unload riders. Wikipedia says 2020 was the first season it did not run at all; it reopened in April 2021. Deno's own site gave the 2026 park opening as April 12. Wikipedia says a ride costs 10 credits, and the cost of each credit varies. Check Deno's site for current prices.
landmarks.source: Wikipedia - Wonder Wheel; Deno's Wonder Wheel directions page

landmarks.name: The Cyclone
landmarks.description: The city bought the Cyclone for $1.2 million in 1969. In 1972 aquarium officials said they would replace it with a swamp display, which started a Save the Cyclone campaign. Astroland won the lease in 1975 at $57,000 a year and reopened it on July 3, 1975. Luna Park has run it since 2011. Wooden coasters can no longer be built under city code, so it cannot be rebuilt. At least three people have died after riding it, in 1985, 1988 and 2007. On August 22, 2024, it stopped mid-ride over a cracked sprocket; riders got off unhurt and it reopened September 7.

landmarks.name: Parachute Jump
landmarks.description: The tower opened at the 1939 New York World's Fair on May 27, 1939, where a ride cost 40 cents for adults and 25 cents for children. It moved to Steeplechase and reopened in May 1941. Most riders went up in just under a minute and dropped in 11 to 15 seconds. It was added to the National Register on September 2, 1980, and became a city landmark on May 23, 1989, the same day as the Wonder Wheel.

landmarks.name: B&B Carousell
landmarks.architect_or_designer: William F. Mangels; horses carved by Marcus Illions
landmarks.description: Wikipedia calls it the last operating carousel in Coney Island. It has 50 horses and 2 chariots and has stood in Luna Park since 2013. Its build date is disputed: Wikipedia says about 1906 to 1909, while a Coney Island History Project caption says 1919. The name comes from William Bishoff and Herman Brienstein, who bought it in 1932. The city's economic development agency paid $1.7 million to restore the horses. It joined the National Register in 2016.
landmarks.source: Wikipedia - B&B Carousell; Coney Island History Project

landmarks.name: Luna Park (2010)
landmarks.description: The current Luna Park opened May 29, 2010, under a 10-year city lease announced that February; Zamperla / Central Amusement International won it. Its 2026 season opened Saturday, March 28. Entry is free and rides started at $4 in 2026; the Luna Park site advertises a Luna Pass from $40 (undated). Wikipedia says rides cannot be paid for in cash. The steel Thunderbolt coaster opened here on June 14, 2014. It borrows the name of a wooden coaster that ran from 1925 to 1982.
landmarks.source: Wikipedia - Luna Park (2010); Time Out New York, Mar 2026; Luna Park site

landmarks.name: Maimonides Park
landmarks.description: The ballpark stands on the old Steeplechase grounds. It was KeySpan Park, then MCU Park, and took the Maimonides name in 2021. Wikipedia says the Brooklyn Cyclones brought pro baseball back to Brooklyn for the first time since the Dodgers left Ebbets Field in 1957. The team is named for the Cyclone coaster. In 2021 the hot dog eating contest moved inside the park because of COVID limits, and Joey Chestnut set the contest record of 76 there. He fell short of it in July 2026.
landmarks.source: Wikipedia - Maimonides Park; Wikipedia - Coney Island Cyclone

landmarks.name: First Symphony of the Sea
landmarks.description: A 332-foot-long, ten-foot-tall cast-concrete sculpture wall on the boardwalk outside the aquarium, installed in 1992. NYC Parks lists it among the park's highlights.
landmarks.source: NYC Parks - Coney Island Beach & Boardwalk highlights

cultural_refs.title: Little Fugitive
cultural_refs.creator: Morris Engel
cultural_refs.description: A 7-year-old boy takes the $6 his mother left for groceries and rides the subway to Coney Island. Coney Island scenes fill two-thirds of the film, shot for $30,000 with a camera strapped to Engel's body. It won the Silver Lion at Venice. François Truffaut said: “Our New Wave would never have come into being if it hadn't been for the young American Morris Engel.”

cultural_refs.title: The Warriors
cultural_refs.creator: Walter Hill
cultural_refs.description: A gang fights its way home to Coney Island after being blamed for a murder it did not commit. It is based on Sol Yurick's 1965 novel. Brooklyn Magazine says the film begins and ends under the Wonder Wheel, with the boardwalk shops shuttered. One character asks: “This is what we fought all night to get back to?”

cultural_refs.title: Annie Hall
cultural_refs.description: Alvy Singer grows up in a house under the Thunderbolt roller coaster that shakes every time the coaster runs. NYC Tourism notes that Molly and George Moran, who ran the original Thunderbolt, really lived in a house under it.

cultural_refs.title: A Coney Island of the Mind
cultural_refs.creator: Lawrence Ferlinghetti
cultural_refs.description: The phrase “a Coney Island of the mind” first appeared in Henry Miller's Black Spring as a put-down: “Everything is sordid, shoddy, thin as pasteboard. A Coney Island of the mind.” Lawrence Ferlinghetti used it as the title of his 1958 poetry book, which has about a million copies in print.

cultural_refs.title: Weegee's Coney Island crowd photograph
cultural_refs.creator: Weegee
cultural_refs.description: The V&A dates Weegee's “Coney Island” beach photograph to 1940. Weegee also shot a crowd picture from an elevated lifeguard station (Whitney Museum). The Whitney notes he did occasional freelance work for the newspaper PM.

cultural_refs.title: Coney Island Baby
cultural_refs.creator: Lou Reed
cultural_refs.description: Lou Reed's album Coney Island Baby was released in December 1975; one Wikipedia list dates it 1976. Reed later served as King Neptune of the Mermaid Parade in 2010, with Laurie Anderson as Queen Mermaid.

cultural_refs.title: She's So Unusual (album cover)
cultural_refs.creator: Cyndi Lauper; photographed by Annie Leibovitz
cultural_refs.description: The cover was shot on Henderson Walk in Coney Island by Annie Leibovitz in 1983.

cultural_refs.title: Coney Island
cultural_refs.creator: Taylor Swift featuring The National
cultural_refs.description: A song titled “Coney Island,” featuring The National, is on Swift's 2020 album evermore.

recurring_events.name: Mermaid Parade
recurring_events.when_text: A Saturday in June, near the summer solstice; held June 20, 2026
recurring_events.description: Coney Island USA started the parade in 1983. The 44th parade was held Saturday, June 20, 2026, at 1 p.m., with about 5,000 marchers, per 6sqft, in handmade sea costumes. The route runs from West 21st Street and Surf Avenue east to West 10th, then west along the boardwalk to Steeplechase Plaza. At 4 p.m., 6sqft says, the king and queen lead a procession to the beach at 19th Street to open the summer swimming season. The 2026 King Neptune and Queen Mermaid were Jesse Malin and Rickie Lee Jones. Money trouble hit the 2026 parade; a GoFundMe raised more than $42,000 and the Borough President pledged $20,000 a year.

recurring_events.name: Nathan's Famous Hot Dog Eating Contest
recurring_events.description: The 2026 contest ran 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Surf and Stillwell. Joey Chestnut, 42, won his 18th men's title with 66 hot dogs in ten minutes. Miki Sudo won her 12th women's title with 38.75. The organizer says the contest dates to 1916, but its promoter admitted in 2010 that he made up that story in the early 1970s. Wikipedia reports the first official contest was June 30, 1967. Nathan's dates its first major recorded contest to July 4, 1972.

recurring_events.name: Polar Bear Club New Year's Day plunge
recurring_events.when_text: January 1; started at 1 p.m. in 2019 and 2022
recurring_events.description: The club began on New Year's Day 1903, when Bernarr Macfadden led about 50 people to the beach for exercises and a swim. The 2019 and 2022 plunges started at 1 p.m. In 2018 the Museum of the City of New York reported that guests must sign a waiver, and it warned of cold-water shock and hypothermia. Check the date and time before you go.

recurring_events.name: Friday night fireworks
recurring_events.when_text: Friday nights in summer, plus July 4
recurring_events.description: Free fireworks run on summer Friday nights, according to NYC Tourism. Start times differ by source: the aquarium says 9:30 p.m., NYC Tourism says 9:45 p.m. Neither source gives 2026 dates, and the summer season has ended.

recurring_events.name: Luna Park opening weekend and Cyclone birthday
recurring_events.description: Luna Park opened its 2026 season on Saturday, March 28. On Sunday, March 29, the first 99 riders got a free Cyclone ride and an egg cream, one for each year of the coaster's age. The count runs toward the Cyclone's 2027 centennial.

businesses.name: Nathan's Famous
businesses.description: The original hot dog stand, still on its 1916 site. The Handwerker family sold all locations to private investors in 1987. On January 21, 2026, Nathan's announced a $450 million sale to Smithfield Foods. We could not confirm whether the sale has closed.
businesses.source: Wikipedia - Nathan's Famous; Major League Eating

businesses.name: New York Aquarium
businesses.description: Founded in Battery Park in 1896, at Coney Island since 1957. At the Coney opening a penguin named Annie cut the ribbon by biting a wrapped smelt. During Hurricane Sandy a small crew stayed and saved 80 percent of the animals; the aquarium fully reopened in July 2022. Its Sharks building opened June 30, 2018. In October 2026 it is running Ascarium weekends.
businesses.source: Wikipedia - New York Aquarium; WNYC; New York Aquarium About page

businesses.name: Coney Island USA: Sideshows by the Seashore and Coney Island Museum
businesses.description: A nonprofit founded in 1980. It calls its theater “the last permanently housed circus sideshow in the USA.” In 2026 sideshow tickets were $15 for adults and $12 for children under 12; a combo with the museum was $18 and $15. The 2026 season is over; the group says it will be back in 2027.
businesses.source: Coney Island USA; Wikipedia - Coney Island USA

businesses.name: Coney Island History Project
businesses.description: An exhibit space next to Deno's Wonder Wheel. For Coney Island's 200th anniversary in 2023 it showed a toll house sign from 1823. Its exhibits ran weekends through October 11 (the page gives no year, probably 2026), so check its site for next season.
businesses.address: 3059 West 12th Street (now Denos Vourderis Place), Brooklyn

things_to_know.label: Swim only in open sections
things_to_know.note: Swimming is not allowed when lifeguards are off duty or in closed sections. Red flags and signs mark closed sections; a red flag means do not swim. Parks posts which sections are open on its beach map soon after 10 a.m. You can also sign up for Notify NYC beach alerts.

things_to_know.label: The season rule
things_to_know.note: NYC beaches are guarded from Memorial Day weekend through the Sunday after Labor Day. Lifeguards take their chairs at 10 a.m. and leave at 6 p.m. Check NYC Parks in spring for the 2027 dates.

things_to_know.label: Water quality after rain
things_to_know.note: The Health Department samples the water weekly, starting a month before the season. Heavy rain can trigger an advisory before test results come back. A yellow sign means swimming and wading are not recommended. A red sign means they are not allowed. The beach itself stays open. If you get sick after swimming, see a doctor and call 311.

things_to_know.label: Rip currents
things_to_know.note: A rip current looks like a calm spot between rougher water on both sides. It pulls you out, not under. If you are caught, stay calm and float on your back. In July 2024, News 12 saw people swimming during red-flag rip warnings with no lifeguards on duty.

things_to_know.label: Rules
things_to_know.note: The boardwalk is closed from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. A May 2025 Fox 5 roundup of all eight city beaches said alcohol and dogs (other than service animals) are not allowed on the beaches, but NYC Parks rules for other beaches limit the dog ban to Memorial Day weekend through October 1. We found no rules page just for Coney Island, so call 311 to check.

things_to_know.label: Wheelchair access
things_to_know.note: Beach mats are at West 33rd, 32nd, 29th and 22nd Streets, Stillwell Avenue, West 5th and 8th Streets and Ocean Parkway. Beach wheelchairs are free for up to three hours, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., in season. Reserve online or by phone, ideally 48 hours ahead. You must leave ID, bring an attendant 18 or older, and stop at the water's edge. Parks lists the phone as (718) 885-2275, the same number it lists for Orchard Beach.

things_to_know.label: Subway and bus
things_to_know.note: Coney Island-Stillwell Avenue is served by the D, F, N and Q trains and is listed as accessible. The F and Q also stop at West 8th Street-NY Aquarium, which Wikipedia calls the southernmost station in the subway system. Buses serving Stillwell include the B36, B64, B68, B74 and B82.

things_to_know.label: Driving and parking
things_to_know.note: NYC Parks lists only metered street parking. From Manhattan, take the Belt Parkway east to exit 7, Ocean Parkway, then Surf Avenue. These directions are from the New York Aquarium. In summer, traffic on Surf Avenue only allows a left turn into the aquarium lot.

access_note: Take the subway. The D, F, N and Q trains end at Coney Island-Stillwell Avenue, a short walk from the boardwalk; the F and Q also stop at West 8th Street-NY Aquarium. JFK airport is about 11 miles away in a straight line. Drivers take the Belt Parkway to Ocean Parkway and Surf Avenue, and parking is metered street spaces only.

travel.title: Plan a Coney Island beach day
travel.kicker: How to get to Coney Island Beach, what the trip costs, when and where you may swim, how to check the water, where the restrooms are, and what is open after the season.
travel.meta_title: Coney Island Beach Day: Subway, Swim Rules, Water Quality
travel.meta_description: Take the D, F, N or Q to Stillwell Avenue. Swim only in open, guarded sections, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. in season. Check the water map first. Full guide inside.
travel.intro:
Coney Island Beach is free, and the subway ends at Coney Island-Stillwell Avenue. The hard part is swimming. You may swim only in sections a lifeguard is watching, only from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., and only during the summer season. Parks said the 2026 season ran through September 13. NYC Health says the city's public beaches reopen Memorial Day weekend 2027.

Beyond the main Coney Island Beach page, this one covers the train and the fare, the daily swim map, water advisories, the rules, restrooms, beach wheelchairs, the off-season and food.

sections.heading: How do you get there by subway, bus or car?
sections.body:
The subway is the easiest way. The D, F, N and Q trains all end at Coney Island-Stillwell Avenue, a terminal station at 1243 Surf Avenue. Wikipedia lists the station as accessible. The F and Q also stop at West Eighth Street-NY Aquarium at all times.

For the New York Aquarium at 602 Surf Avenue, take the F or Q to West 8th Street, or take the N or D to Stillwell and walk two blocks east on Surf Avenue.

Wikipedia lists the B36, B64, B68, B74 and B82 local buses and the X28 and X38 express buses at Stillwell.

The subway and local bus fare is $3, up from $2.90 in January 2026; a seven-day cap is $35. ABC7 reported this in September 2025, after the MTA board vote; the new fare was expected to start January 4, 2026. Our sources give no travel time from Midtown, so use a trip planner.

If you drive, NYC Parks lists only metered street parking. Fox 5 NY said in May 2025 that Brighton Beach, which it lists together with the Coney Island Boardwalk, has metered parking. Neither source names lots or rates.

sections.heading: When is the beach open, and when are lifeguards on duty?
sections.body:
You can visit the sand in any month, but lifeguards work only in summer. NYC Parks' standing rule is that the beach season runs from Memorial Day weekend through the Sunday after Labor Day. Lifeguards are on duty every day of the season from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

In 2026, Brooklyn's beaches were set to open on Saturday, May 23, at 10 a.m., according to a May 2026 preview. Parks said the season ran through September 13, a week after Labor Day, with lifeguards on duty from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

For 2027, NYC Health says public beaches reopen Memorial Day weekend. Our sources do not yet show exact 2027 dates, so check the NYC Parks beaches page in spring.

Lifeguard hours are swim hours. Before 10 a.m. and after 6 p.m., swimming is not allowed anywhere on the beach. How many sections open also depends on staffing. Brownstoner reported in May 2026 that lifeguard shortages in recent years had closed sections of beach for a while, and sometimes for weeks.

sections.heading: Where can you swim, and how does the daily map work?
sections.body:
You may swim only in sections that are open and guarded. NYC Parks says swimming is prohibited when lifeguards are off duty and in closed sections. Closed sections are marked with signs or red flags. A red flag means do not swim.

The open sections change from day to day. In summer, Parks posts an online beach map. It updates each morning soon after 10 a.m., based on how many lifeguards are available and on conditions in the water. A section that was open yesterday may be closed today.

Check the Parks map after 10 a.m. Walk to an open section and look for red flags before you go in. Leave the water when lifeguards tell you to. You can also sign up for Notify NYC beach alerts, which send openings and closings as they happen.

sections.heading: How do you check the water before you go?
sections.body:
The Health Department tests the water, separate from the lifeguard schedule. It takes samples at Coney Island every week, starting one month before the season. The city's beach water quality map is at maps.nyc.gov/beach.

There are two warning levels. An advisory, shown with a yellow sign, means swimming and wading are not recommended. A closure, shown with a red sign, means swimming and wading are not allowed.

Rain matters most. An advisory can start when rain goes past a set threshold for that beach, before test results come back. During an advisory, the beach stays open. Only the water is off limits.

In July 2026, after a week of heavy rain, the city warned people to stay out of the water at a dozen beaches. Coney Island's sample from July 6 read 227 enterococci per 100 milliliters. The New York State limit for a single sample is 104. Enterococci are a warning sign of fecal pollution and more dangerous germs.

Do not count on a sign on the sand. During that advisory, ABC7 found no announcements on the beach and one small sign on the boardwalk. Check the map or Notify NYC yourself. If you get sick after swimming, the Health Department says to see a doctor promptly and report it by calling 311.

sections.heading: What should you know about rip currents and swimming after hours?
sections.body:
Experts give one main rule: do not go in the water when no lifeguards are on duty. After a 2024 drowning here, Gothamist said that was the most important warning from experts.

Know what a rip current looks like. The Swim Strong Foundation told CBS that a rip looks like a calm spot between rough water on either side. It pulls you out, not under. If you are caught, stay calm and float on your back. Parks' beach page links to rip-current tips from the National Weather Service.

Two deaths described in our sources happened in water where swimming was not allowed, in 2023 and 2024. On July 5, 2024, two sisters, ages 17 and 18, went in amid rip-current warnings after lifeguards had gone off duty. Police said they disappeared from view shortly after 8 p.m. On July 27, 2023, a 15-year-old drowned in a no-swimming area near West 22nd Street that Parks said was under a red flag.

Night swimming is not allowed. In May 2026, Parks Commissioner Tricia Shimamura said Coney Island is the only place where Parks runs a 24-hour operation. Swimming is still prohibited whenever lifeguards are off duty.

sections.heading: What are the beach rules?
sections.body:
We found no rules page just for Coney Island Beach. Here is what we can confirm.

NYC Parks' Coney Island beach page says you may swim only when lifeguards are on duty and only in open sections. It also says the boardwalk is closed from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. The city's beach map says that when swimming is closed, you may still walk, run and sit on the sand and boardwalk during regular park hours.

We found no alcohol or dog rule written for Coney Island Beach. Fox 5 NY reported in May 2025, citing NYC Parks, that alcohol and dogs other than service animals are not permitted on the city's public beaches. That is a press summary for all eight city beaches. NYC Parks' own rules pages for two other beaches, Orchard Beach in the Bronx and Manhattan Beach in Brooklyn, limit the dog ban to Memorial Day weekend through October 1, so the dog rule may depend on the season. Our sources say nothing about glass, grills or smoking at Coney Island. Before you bring alcohol, a dog or any of those, call 311.

Every May and June, horseshoe crabs come ashore on Coney Island Beach, NYC Parks says. If you find one stuck on its back, it is fine to flip it over. Never pick one up by the tail, which will not grow back if it breaks.

In season, NYC Parks runs a free sunscreen program at all eight city beaches, according to its Coney Island page.

sections.heading: Where are the restrooms, and how do wheelchair users reach the sand?
sections.body:
NYC Open Data lists eight restroom zones at Coney Island Beach, all run by NYC Parks. Two are listed as open year-round and six as seasonal. All eight list hours of 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., open later in season. Six of the eight list changing stations. The data names zones, not streets, so it cannot tell you which zone is which building.

NYC Parks also has pages for three named restrooms on the boardwalk: at West 33rd Street, at West 27th Street, and between Brighton 1st Road and Brighton 2nd Street. The West 33rd and West 27th Street restrooms each list one changing table in the men's room and one in the women's room. The Brighton page leaves the changing-table count blank. The three restroom pages do not give hours or say whether the restroom is open in the off-season, and the Open Data list is undated. Only the Brighton page lists its restroom as wheelchair accessible; the other two pages do not say. The Open Data list marks all eight zones fully accessible, but it does not say which zone matches which restroom.

Parks also lists spray showers and a concession stand, but not where they are.

NYC Parks calls Coney Island an accessible beach, with beach mats and free beach wheelchairs by reservation in season. The mats are at West 33rd, West 32nd, West 29th and West 22nd Streets, Stillwell Avenue, West 5th and West 8th Streets, and Ocean Parkway. Wheelchair pickup points are at the same eight streets.

Beach wheelchairs have three oversized wheels and must be pushed by someone else. They are free for up to three hours, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily, from Memorial Day through the Sunday after Labor Day. Parks asks for 48 hours' notice and may fill a same-day request on site if a chair is free. You must leave an ID with Parks staff. An attendant 18 or older must come along. The chair may go only to the water's edge.

Book online if you can. Parks' form also gives (718) 885-2275, but Parks' beaches list shows that number for Orchard Beach in the Bronx, so it may be a citywide line or a copy error. Confirm online. Parks says to check back two days before Memorial Day weekend to reserve a chair for next summer.

sections.heading: What is open after the season, and where can you eat?
sections.body:
The beach and boardwalk stay open after September for walking, not swimming. The boardwalk is closed from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. NYC Parks suggests a walk on the Riegelmann Boardwalk and a look up at the Parachute Jump.

The New York Aquarium's website promotes Ascarium events in October 2026, with animal chats, pumpkin sculptures and bubble shows included with admission. Our sources do not give its fall hours, so check nyaquarium.com before you go.

Some places had closed for the year by mid-October 2026. Coney Island USA said its 2026 sideshow season was over and it would be back in 2027. Our sources do not give fall hours for Luna Park or the Wonder Wheel, so check their own sites.

For food, here is what our sources say. None gives fall hours, so call or check each website before you go. Nathan's Famous still runs its original stand on its 1916 site at Surf and Stillwell Avenues, 1310 Surf Avenue, where it hosted the July 4, 2026 hot dog contest. Wikipedia says fried frog legs are sold only at this location. In January 2026 Nathan's announced a sale to Smithfield Foods; it was expected to close in the first half of 2026, and our sources do not say whether it did.

Luna Park said it refreshed its food options for 2026. Totonno's pizzeria at 1524 Neptune Avenue, open since 1924 by its own account, said in May 2024 that its owners were looking for a buyer. We could not confirm it is open today, so call before you go.

history.title: How Coney Island's Beach Became Public
history.kicker: The story of who owned Coney Island's sand, from a 1654 deed to a 2025 casino vote, and how the beach became public.
history.meta_title: Coney Island Beach History: How the Sand Became Public
history.meta_description: Coney Island's beach was private and fenced until a 1913 court ruling and the city's 1921 title made it public. The story from the 1654 deed to 2025.
history.intro:
Coney Island's beach became public because New York State went to court and the city took title to the land. In 1912 the state sued amusement owners over the beach, and in 1913 a court ruled it belonged to the state. On October 1, 1921, the city took title to the shore and broke ground on the boardwalk. Before that, private owners had split up the waterfront and fenced off parts of the sand.

This page tells the story from the name to the 2025 casino fight. The story of Steeplechase, Luna Park and Dreamland is on the main Coney Island Beach page.

Where sources disagree, this page says so.

sections.heading: Where does the name Coney Island come from?
sections.body:
Nobody knows for sure. Wikipedia says no theory has strong evidence. The most popular one points to the Dutch word for rabbit.

Dutch maps labeled the sand spit Conyne Eylandt, starting with the 1639 Manatus map. The same map marks a Munsee village named Techkonis. The word history site WordOrigins.org says it may be the source of the “konis” sound, but nothing else is known about that village.

The English name Conyne Island appears as early as May 7, 1654, in a deed. That deed passed the island from the Lenape to settlers of the town of Gravesend. It records the Lenape name narriockh as meaning simply “the island.” Wikipedia says it may mean “land without shadows.” WordOrigins calls that translation spurious.

One other story does not hold up. John Colman, a crewman of Henry Hudson, did die on Coney Island in 1609, but nothing ties him to the name.

In 1679 to 1680, a Dutch journal said: “Nobody lives upon it, but it is used in winter for keeping cattle, horses, oxen, hogs and others.”

sections.heading: When did Coney Island stop being an island?
sections.body:
Coney Island is now a peninsula, but the change happened in steps over many years. In 1750 the Jamaica Ditch was dug through Coney Hook, which split the area into separate islands. That ditch is the start of Coney Island Creek.

In 1824 a company built the first bridge across the ditch, linking the island to the mainland. In the 1830s and 1840s, carriage roads and steamships cut the trip from half a day to two hours.

Then the creek was filled in, piece by piece. Wikipedia says landowners had filled part of the creek by 1924, that Belt Parkway work in the 1930s filled more, and that more fill was added in 1962 for the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge. Because the filling took decades, sources date the change differently, so no single year fits.

sections.heading: What were the first hotels and resorts like?
sections.body:
Wikipedia calls the Coney Island House the first hotel on the island. Its founding date is disputed. NYC Parks' historical sign says 1824. Wikipedia says 1829.

More visitors came as the trip got easier. In 1847 a ferry line to Norton's Point started, and the middle class began to come. Wikipedia says the first railroad reached the island in 1864. By 1904, five railroads served the island.

Big hotels grew at the east end. William Engeman built a resort at Brighton Beach in 1868. In April 1888 the Brighton Beach Hotel was moved 495 feet inland on railroad tracks. The move took nine days. Wikipedia calls it the largest building relocation of the 19th century.

Further east, Austin Corbin built Manhattan Beach. A local history site, Heart of Coney Island, says the town of Gravesend sold him about 500 acres of shoreline for $1,500, or about $3 an acre. In 1895 Corbin added a concrete cycling track for 12,000 people, built for $30,000. Corbin barred Jewish guests from his hotel, and Wikipedia says the policy ended after his death.

One odd building was the Elephantine Colossus, a hotel shaped like an elephant. It was reported to cost $65,000. Its size is disputed. Wikipedia says 122 feet and seven stories. The Brooklyn Public Library says twelve stories with 31 rooms.

sections.heading: Who ran Coney Island in the Gravesend years?
sections.body:
John Y. McKane was the boss of the town of Gravesend, which sold shoreline on Coney Island. Most of what follows comes from Heart of Coney Island, a local history site, so treat the numbers as its account.

The site says McKane's construction company was credited with building nearly two-thirds of the buildings in Coney Island and Gravesend. In the 1893 election his machine turned in 2,700 votes in a town with 1,700 registered voters. When Republican poll watchers came with a court injunction, McKane told them: “Injunctions don't go here!” In 1894 he was sentenced to six years in Sing Sing for election fraud. He died in 1899, the site says.

Robert Moses, the city's parks chief, gave his own blunt view in a recorded speech in the 1950s. He said Coney had been “town land owned by the people, given away to crooks for a song.”

sections.heading: How did the fenced beach become public?
sections.body:
The main page tells how private fences gave way to a public beach. Here are details it leaves out.

The 1913 ruling did not settle everything. When an appeals court upheld it in 1916, it made an exception for part of Steeplechase Park. The boardwalk then opened in stages. A first section opened in October 1922. An extension to West 17th Street followed that December. The last stretch, from West 17th to West 37th Street, opened on May 15, 1923.

Sources differ on the cost. NYC Parks' sign puts the beach work and boardwalk at $3 million. Wikipedia says the boardwalk and related projects cost $20 million in all.

Parks took over the boardwalk in 1938. Wikipedia quotes Robert Moses saying that city beaches and boardwalks “were never properly planned.” In a 1950s speech, Moses said that when the city took over Coney Island in 1937, it had only about 50 acres of shrinking, overcrowded beach. “Often at high tide there was no beach at all,” he said.

sections.heading: What were the crowded years like?
sections.body:
The subway made Coney Island a nickel trip. New York subway fares stayed at five cents from 1904 to 1948, according to the Barry Popik blog. An Atlas Obscura line says the fare to Coney Island dropped from ten cents to five in 1920. That clashes with the fare history. The 1920 date is when the BMT subway reached Coney Island.

The cheap ride changed the east end. Wikipedia says the new subway made day trips easy and led to the closing of the Brighton Beach Hotel in 1924. Fortune magazine wrote in 1938 that this “Nickel Empire” peaked in the mid-1920s. Still, NYC Parks says that even in the Great Depression, Coney Island drew millions of visitors.

In July 1932 a fire that the Brooklyn Paper says is considered the worst in Coney Island's history burned 100 feet of the boardwalk. Thousands of bathers ran out of the burning bathhouses and were left on the beach without their clothes. Historian Charles Denson blames children playing with matches.

sections.heading: What happened after World War II?
sections.body:
In the 1940s and 1950s, the city's plans for Coney Island turned to housing and a new aquarium. Robert Moses pushed both. On April 2, 1953, the New York Times reported that he had proposed rezoning Coney Island for homes.

The aquarium needed a new home because Moses wanted the old one gone. In 1941 he called the Battery Park aquarium “an ugly wart on the main axis leading straight to the Statue of Liberty.” WNYC says the Battery Park aquarium closed on October 1, 1941. It also says the cornerstone at Coney Island was laid in 1954 and the aquarium reopened in 1957. The website 6sqft says Moses moved it to the old Dreamland site in 1947. That year was more likely a plan than an opening.

Housing towers rose where amusements had stood. A neighborhood guide lists the Coney Island Houses in 1956 and the Warbasse Houses in 1966. In 1974 the housing group CHPC wrote a report in response to a court order to desegregate Mark Twain Junior High School. It argued that the whole neighborhood had to be made more attractive. Bobby Nagy, in an oral history, remembered 1970s Coney Island as “dirty and scary and rough,” yet still alluring.

Astroland kept rides running. It opened in 1962 on 3.1 acres. Wikipedia says an early-morning fire on July 12, 1975 wiped out much of the park, and it was rebuilt. Dick Zigun, a founder of Coney Island USA, recalled that owner Jerry Albert bragged Astroland had “not one light bulb burned out.” The Albert family sold Astroland to Thor Equities on November 28, 2006, for $30 million. Wikipedia says Thor announced a $1.5 billion year-round resort that never came to be.

sections.heading: What has happened since 2009?
sections.body:
The fights since 2009 have been about who controls the land between Surf Avenue and the boardwalk. Charles Denson, a Coney Island historian, said in 2016 about his Steeplechase demolition exhibit: “To me the real business in Coney Island has always been real estate.”

On July 29, 2009, the City Council approved a rezoning of the amusement district. It made a 27-acre amusement district, but kept only 12 acres for outdoor rides. The rest could hold indoor amusements and up to four hotels. On November 25, 2009, the Save Coney Island coalition sued, saying the plan favored Thor Equities. The city bought much of the amusement zone from Thor's Joe Sitt for $100 million, and Thor kept about four acres. The city gave Central Amusement International a 10-year lease. In 2010 the landlord, Central Amusement International, ordered Ruby's Bar and eight other boardwalk businesses to leave by November 15.

Hurricane Sandy hit in October 2012. The Army Corps of Engineers says the elevated beach avoided an estimated $494 million in damage to houses and structures during the storm. Marine Technology Reporter says the surge also pushed sand and water over the boardwalk, and the beach lost 600,000 cubic yards of sand. In 2013 the Corps placed about 580,000 cubic yards of sand to restore the beach's authorized design. In September 2022 the Army Corps released a draft flood plan for New York and parts of New Jersey. The plan is priced at $52 billion for the whole region. The Coney Island History Project says it would raise the boardwalk five feet with what appears to be a wide concrete walkway that acts as a surge barrier. A 2022 post from the History Project says construction would begin in 2030. This page found no source on its status after 2023.

The most recent fight this page found was over a casino. The Coney was a $3 billion plan beside the boardwalk, with a 500-room hotel. In January 2025 a Community Board 13 committee voted 7 to 2 against it, with one abstention. One supporter said Coney Island had been “promised so much for so many decades, and nothing came about.” On September 29, 2025, a state advisory committee voted 4 to 2 against it. Borough President Antonio Reynoso voted no, saying it “failed to prove itself as a public good.” Politics NY reported that on December 1, 2025, the state gaming location board voted unanimously for the three remaining bids, in the Bronx and Queens. Coney Island was not among them. The report said the state gaming commission would rule within the month. This page found no source on that ruling. Brownstoner reported that the City Council's 2025 rezoning for the casino would be reversed. This page could not confirm the current zoning.

Today, NYC Parks says all city public beaches are free and open to the public.

the-rides.title: The rides still standing at Coney Island
the-rides.kicker: What you can still see and ride at Coney Island, and how each old ride survived.
the-rides.meta_title: Coney Island's Old Rides: Wonder Wheel, Cyclone, Parachute Jump
the-rides.meta_description: Coney Island still runs the 1920 Wonder Wheel, the 1927 Cyclone and a restored carousel. See how each ride survived, who saved it and where sources differ.
the-rides.intro:
Three old rides still carry riders at Coney Island: the Wonder Wheel from 1920, the Cyclone roller coaster from 1927, and the B&B Carousell. A fourth, the Parachute Jump, still stands on the boardwalk but no longer carries anyone. Two parks run the rides today. Deno's Wonder Wheel Park is run by the Vourderis family, Wikipedia says. Luna Park, opened in 2010, runs the Cyclone, the carousel and the newer steel Thunderbolt.

The Cyclone, the carousel and the Parachute Jump each came close to being lost, and each was saved a different way. The Wonder Wheel changed hands in 1983, when the Vourderis family bought it. Astroland leased the Cyclone after the city planned to tear it down. A private donor bought the carousel for the city. The Parachute Jump stayed up after a city auction drew no bids. This page tells how each survived, what each is like to ride, and where the sources disagree on heights and dates.

sections.heading: What could you ride in 2026?
sections.body:
Luna Park opened its 2026 season on Saturday, March 28, Time Out New York reported. The Cyclone ran that first weekend. On Sunday, March 29, the first 99 riders got a free ride and an egg cream.

Sources differ on when Deno's opened in 2026. A Brownstoner article in May said Luna Park and Deno's both opened in March. Deno's website gave April 12, with kiddie rides at 11 a.m. and adult rides at noon. We could not settle it.

The Parachute Jump has not been a ride since the 1960s. It stands on the boardwalk between West 16th and West 19th Streets, in Steeplechase Plaza.

Both parks run on a seasonal schedule. In October 2026 we could not confirm either park's fall hours. Deno's website listed its daily summer season as May 25 through September 8. In 2016, Atlas Obscura described the Wonder Wheel as running from about Easter to Halloween, but that is old. Check each park's own site before you go.

sections.heading: The Wonder Wheel: one family's wheel since 1983
sections.body:
The Wonder Wheel opened on Memorial Day 1920. It is 150 feet tall and has 24 cabins. Eight are fixed to the rim, like a normal Ferris wheel. The other 16 slide inward on winding tracks as the wheel turns, then swing back out. Each kind has its own line.

Each rotation takes ten minutes, and a ride is two rotations. The wheel can carry 864 riders an hour. Its busiest day was July 4, 1947, when it carried 14,506 people.

Fred Garms and his cousin Walter Kerner Sr. sold the wheel to Denos Vourderis in 1983. Atlas Obscura says Vourderis was born in Aigion, Greece, in 1920, the eighth of 22 children. He came to the United States at 14 and first sold hot dogs from a pushcart in Manhattan. Wikipedia calls Deno's the last family-operated amusement park in Coney Island and says the family has turned down offers to sell. The street in front, once West 12th Street, is now Denos Vourderis Place.

A ticket rose from 50 cents in 1976 to $1.25 in 1981. Hurricane Sandy flooded Deno's park in 2012, but the wheel was only slightly damaged and reopened the next year.

The wheel became New York City Landmark no. 1708 on May 23, 1989. Atlas Obscura says it joined the National Register of Historic Places in 1984. Wikipedia gives no National Register date, so we could not confirm that one. Wikipedia calls it the oldest continuously operating ride at Coney Island. But it did not run at all in 2020, the first lost season in its history, so it has not run every year.

sections.heading: The Cyclone: the coaster the city planned to tear down
sections.body:
The Cyclone is a wooden roller coaster designed by Vernon Keenan. It opened on June 26, 1927, and cost a reported $146,000 to $175,000 to build. A ride was 25 cents, or 35 cents on Sundays and holidays.

Sources do not agree on its size. Wikipedia says it is 75 feet tall. It says the 85 feet you often see is measured to the sign above the lift hill. Luna Park's own page gives an 85-foot plunge and calls it the second-steepest wooden coaster in the world. Wikipedia ranked its drop ninth-steepest as of 2014. Ride time differs too: about one minute 50 seconds in Wikipedia's text, 2:30 in its infobox, and 2 minutes per NYC Tourism.

Each train seats 24 riders, two across, with lap bars and no headrests. Only one of the three trains runs at a time. In 2026, riders had to be 54 inches tall.

After the city bought the ride in 1969, it soon piled up 101 safety violations. The main page tells how the aquarium then planned to replace it. When Astroland won the lease in 1975, it spent $60,000 on repairs. The Brooklyn Paper wrote in 2012 that the Albert family, who ran Astroland, "rushed to Coney's rescue" when the city decided to demolish the coaster.

The Cyclone became New York City Landmark no. 1636 in 1988. Wikipedia's infobox says June 12, 1988, but its own reference dates the landmark report July 12, 1988. It joined the National Register on June 25, 1991. Luna Park took over the ride in 2011. Great Coasters International finished a refurbishment in 2016. After the ride stopped mid-run in August 2024, the city cited Luna Park for two violations.

NYC Tourism retells a 1948 New York Times report that a mute man, Emilio Franco, got his voice back on the ride. His first words were that he felt sick. In August 1977, 19-year-old Richard Rodriguez rode it for 104 hours, eating hot dogs and M&Ms between rides. Photographer Lily Binder called it "the most physically and mentally cleansing minute of your life because you can't think."

Each opening weekend, Luna Park gives free rides and egg creams to as many riders as the coaster is years old. It was 98 riders in 2025 and 99 in 2026, counting down to the Cyclone's centennial in 2027.

sections.heading: The Parachute Jump: why a closed ride still stands
sections.body:
The Parachute Jump is a 250-foot, 170-ton open steel tower with twelve arms. At the 1939 World's Fair a pole on top made it 262 feet tall. It came to Steeplechase Park in 1941. 6sqft calls it all that remains of Steeplechase.

Sources disagree on the year it last carried riders. Coney Island historian Charles Denson and the Coney Island History Project say 1964 and call 1968 a repeated error. The Brooklyn Paper says it was shut in 1965, and a 1965 Daily News article said it had been stripped of its wires and chutes. NYC Parks' website and engineer Helen Harrison say 1968. Harrison says its last documented incident was May 30, 1968. We follow Denson's 1964, since his group studies the site, but 1968 still appears widely.

The main page tells how Fred Trump wanted to sell the tower for scrap and how a 1971 auction drew no bids. Before that, in 1966, the Coney Island Chamber of Commerce asked the Landmarks Commission to protect it.

The tower now holds three listings. It joined the National Register on September 2, 1980, and the state register on October 23, 1981. It became New York City Landmark no. 1638 on May 23, 1989, the same day as the Wonder Wheel. A 2018 article on 6sqft says it was named a landmark in 1977. That date does not match any of the dated listings, so we use 1989 for the city landmark.

The tower has lights for night shows. Its lights were switched on in 2006 and replaced in 2013. The frame carries about 8,000 fixtures for light shows. It has been lit in memory of events such as Kobe Bryant's death.

sections.heading: The B&B Carousell: bought for the city, restored in Ohio
sections.body:
The B&B Carousell was built by Coney Island maker William F. Mangels, with wooden horses carved by Marcus Illions. Its build date is disputed. Wikipedia, drawing on the National Register nomination, says about 1906 to 1909. A Coney Island History Project caption says 1919. Wikipedia's date comes from the National Register nomination, so it is probably the better one, but we could not rule out 1919.

It has 50 horses and 2 chariots. Thirty-six of the horses move up and down.

The carousel nearly left Coney Island. Developer Joe Sitt bought the land under it. When the lease ran out, he evicted the operator, McCullough. In 2005 a private donor bought the carousel for the city. The horses went to Ohio for restoration from 2008 to 2013, paid for with $1.7 million from the city's economic development agency. The carousel has stood in Luna Park since 2013. It joined the National Register on February 23, 2016. Wikipedia calls it the last operating carousel in Coney Island.

sections.heading: Luna Park and the Thunderbolt: what replaced Astroland
sections.body:
Today's Luna Park stands where Astroland stood. Astroland opened in 1962 on 3.1 acres at 1000 Surf Avenue. Its space theme came from John Glenn's orbit, and early rides simulated trips to the moon for 50 cents. On November 28, 2006, the Albert family sold Astroland to Thor Equities for $30 million. Thor announced a $1.5 billion year-round resort that was never built. Astroland closed on September 7, 2008.

The city then bought a large part of the amusement zone from Joe Sitt for $100 million, the Brooklyn Paper reported in 2010. Mayor Bloomberg announced on February 16, 2010, that Zamperla and Central Amusement International had won a 10-year lease on the 3.16-acre site. Luna Park opened on May 29, 2010.

One Astroland ride lingered. On July 2, 2013, Luna Park was evacuated because the old AstroTower was swaying. Crews cut the top down overnight, the park reopened at 3 p.m. on July 4, and by July 6 only a four-foot stump was left. The Astroland rocket now sits as a monument inside Deno's Wonder Wheel Park.

The park has grown since. A 2018 city plan for a log flume, zip line and ropes course would enlarge it by 50 percent and add 100 jobs. Building began in October 2021, and four new rides opened in June 2023, including the Tony's Express coaster and the Leti's Treasure log flume. Wikipedia's counts of the park's rides do not agree with each other: 36 attractions in one place and 28 in its infobox. The park is also larger now than the 3.16-acre site in the 2010 lease, because it was expanded later.

The steel Thunderbolt opened on June 14, 2014, after delays that began at Memorial Day. It is a $9 million Zamperla ride with a 90-degree drop and four inversions. Each train is one car with nine seats, three rows of three. In 2026, riders had to be 50 inches tall. Sources give slightly different numbers. Wikipedia lists 2,234 feet of track and a top speed of 56 mph, and Luna Park lists 2,233 feet. NYC Tourism lists 55 mph. Drop height is 112 feet in Wikipedia and 115 feet in NYC Tourism.

The name is borrowed. The first Thunderbolt was a wooden coaster that George Moran ran from 1925 to 1982. Luna Park says only that it ran into the early 1980s. It was torn down in 2000. Molly and George Moran lived in a house under the coaster.

sections.heading: What should you check before you go?
sections.body: We could not find out what happened to Luna Park's city lease after its first 10-year term would have ended in 2020. Prices, ride lists and hours change each year. Check lunaparknyc.com and denoswonderwheel.com for fall hours and for 2027 before you go.
